# Quantitative partial regularity of the Navier-Stokes equations and applications

# Abstract

We prove a logarithmic improvement of the Caffarelli-Kohn-Nirenberg partial regularity theorem for the Navier-Stokes equations. The key idea is to find a quantitative counterpart for the absolute continuity of the dissipation energy using the pigeonhole principle. Based on the same method, for any suitable weak solution, we show the existence of intervals of regularity in one spatial direction with length depending exponentially on the natural local energies of the solution. Then, we give two applications of the latter result in the axially symmetric case. The first one is a local quantitative regularity criterion for suitable weak solutions with small swirl. The second one is a slightly improved one-point CKN criterion which implies all known (slightly supercritical) Type I regularity results in the literature.

# 1 Introduction

We study the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations in three dimensions:

$$\tag{NS}
\left\{
\begin{aligned}
  \partial_t v - \Delta v + (v \cdot \nabla) v + \nabla p &= 0,\\
  \nabla \cdot v &= 0,\\
\end{aligned}
\right.$$

where $v,p$ are the unknown velocity and pressure fields. Whether the solutions to (1) can develop finite time singularities from regular initial data remains a question of central importance in the theory of partial differential equations. It has been called one of the seven most important unsolved problems by the Clay Mathematics Institute, see [11].

In 1934, based on the natural energy structure of (1), Leray [19] constructed global weak solutions for the Cauchy problem of (1) with finite kinetic energy $\sup_{t\ge 0} \int_{\R^3} |v|^2 dx$ and finite dissipation energy (Dirichlet integral) $\int_0^{+\infty} \int_{\R^3} |\nabla v|^2 dx dt.$ Moreover, for these solutions the global energy inequality

$$\int_{\R^3 \times \{t\}} |v|^2 dx + 2 \int_{0}^t \int_{\R^3} |\nabla v|^2 dxdt \le \int_{\R^3 \times \{0\}} |v|^2 dx \tag{1}$$

holds for a.a. $t > 0$. Later, Hopf [12] obtained a similar existence result for the boundary value problem of (1) on bounded domains. As well-known, (1) enjoys a natural scaling invariance property, namely, for any solution $(v,p)$ to (1), the rescaled functions

$$v^{(\lambda)}(x,t) = \lambda v(\lambda x, \lambda^2 t), \ p^{(\lambda)}(x,t) = \lambda^2 p(\lambda x, \lambda^2 t) \tag{2}$$

also satisfy (1) for any $\lambda > 0$. The kinetic and dissipation energies of (1) are both supercritical with respect to the natural scaling of (1), namely, the energies of the zoomed-in solution $v^{(\lambda)}$ with $\lambda < 1$ are greater than those of the original solution $v$. This indicates that the a priori estimates of the Leray-Hopf weak solutions are too weak to control the behavior of $v$ on fine scales.

In the papers [27, 28], Scheffer initiated the study of partial regularity for the Navier-Stokes equations, that is, to estimate the dimension of the potential singular set of a weak solution. He considered a subclass of the Leray-Hopf weak solutions satisfying the local energy inequality, and proved that the singular set is of Hausdorff dimension no more than $\frac53$. In the landmark work of Caffarelli, Kohn and Nirenberg [3], Scheffer’s result is improved, and it is shown that the 1d parabolic Hausdorff measure of the singular set is equal to $0$ for a class of suitable weak solutions. [3] is a foundation for many important results later, *e.g.*, the $L^\infty_t L^3_x$ regularity criterion [9], backward and forward self-similar solutions [26, 14], regularity via Liouville theorems [16], *etc*. Simplified proofs of the partial regularity theorem are given by Lin [20], Ladyzhenskaya-Seregin [17] and Vasseur [35]. To describe the theory precisely, we recall a few important notions.

Although it is not clear whether all Leray-Hopf weak solutions are suitable, in the appendix of [3] the authors were able to construct suitable Leray-Hopf weak solutions for the Cauchy problem and the boundary value problem of (1) with general $L^2$ initial data. See also [20, Lemma 2.3] or [17, Theorem 1.1] for the a priori estimates on the pressure.

The classical partial regularity theorem of Caffarelli-Kohn-Nirenberg reads

The proof of Theorem 1 is based on the important $\e$-regularity criterion. Using the a priori bounds in Definition 1 and interpolation, we know that $v \in L_t^{s}L_x^{l}(Q(1))$ for any $s ,l$ satisfying $\frac{2}{s}+\frac{3}{l} = \frac{3}{2}$, $l \in [2, 6]$. We define the functionals

$$\G = \G[v,p] \stackrel{\Delta}= \int_{Q(1)} \left(|v|^3 + |p|^{3/2} \right) dxdt < +\infty \tag{3}$$

and

$$\H = \H[v] \stackrel{\Delta}= \int_{Q(1)} |\nabla v|^2 dxdt < +\infty \tag{4}$$

for a suitable weak solution $(v,p)$. By (1), the kinetic and the dissipation energies of $v$ on $Q(r)$ for any $r<1$ are bounded in terms of $\G[v,p]$.

We refer to [3, 20, 17, 35] for proofs of the Hölder continuity of $v$ in Theorem 1, and to [22, Proposition 2.1] for a remark on how to obtain the higher regularity estimates. Note that the methods in [20, 17] rely on certain (non-quantitative) compactness arguments, while the method in [35] based on the De Giorgi iteration is quantitative. With the help of Theorem 1 and an iteration of scale-invariant quantities, the one-point regularity criterion Theorem 1 can be established. Then, Theorem 1 is a corollary of Theorem 1 and the absolute continuity of the dissipation energy $\int |\nabla v|^2 dxdt$.

We point out that the proof of Theorem 1 in [3] is still non-quantitative, essentially because the absolute continuity of the dissipation energy is a non-quantitative fact. Given any integrable function $g$ on $Q(1)$, it is well-known that for any $\e > 0$, there exists $\delta > 0$ such that $\int_U |g| dxdt < \e$ for any $U$ with $|U| \stackrel{\Delta}= \int_U 1 dxdt < \delta$. However, it is clearly impossible to give an explicit dependence of $\delta$ on $\epsilon$ unless higher integrability of $g$ is assumed.

Remarkably, Choe and Lewis [8] improved Theorem 1 for the first time and showed that $\mathcal{P}^{f} (\mathcal{S}[v]) = 0$ for $f(r) = r|\ln r|^\alpha$ for a small positive $\alpha$ (precisely $0 \le \alpha<\frac{3}{44}$). The key step is to show that $\ln (1/d) |\nabla v|^2$ is locally integrable where $d$ is the parabolic distance to certain subsets of the singular set. See also the work [25] for an improvement on the range of $\alpha$.

For any singular point $w = (x,t) \in S[v]$, we say that $w$ is Type I if

$$\limsup_{r \to 0+}\frac{1}{r} \int_{Q(r,w)} |\nabla v|^2 dxdt < + \infty. \tag{5}$$

For $w = (0,0)$, the pointwise upper bound

$$|v| \le \frac{C_*}{\sqrt{|x|^2-t}}, \ \mbox{for} \ (x,t) \in Q(r), \ r>0 \tag{6}$$

would imply (5). It is a major open problem in the field to rule out the possibility of blow-up under the condition (5) or (6). In other words, it is of great importance to improve the CKN criterion Theorem 1, in particular, to *remove the smallness requirement* there.

## 1.1 Main results

### 1.1.1 Quantitative partial regularity

In this paper, we first give a further improvement on the partial regularity theorem using a different approach from [8].

The key idea is to find a sharp quantitative counterpart for the absolute continuity property of the dissipation energy $\int |\nabla v|^2 dxdt$. For any integrable function $g$ defined on an open set $\Omega \subset \R^n$ and any sequence of open sets $U_k \subset \Omega$, consider the quantities

$$\EE_k = \int_{U_k \setminus U_{k+1}} |g| dx. \tag{7}$$

Clearly, $\EE_k$ satisfies the non-overlapping property

$$\sum_{k \ge 1} \EE_k \le \int_{\Omega} |g| dx, \tag{8}$$

which enables the application of the pigeonhole principle. In particular, we have a sequence of $k_j \to +\infty$ such that $\EE_{k_j} \le o(\frac{1}{k_j \ln k_j})$. We will take $g = |\nabla v|^2$, and this observation provides a crucial extra smallness leading to the improvement of partial regularity.

Another ingredient in the proof of Theorem 1.1.1 is to obtain an iteration of the scale-invariant quantities $A(r)$, $E(r)$, $F(r)$ and $D(r)$ (see Section 2.1) based on the energy structure of the Navier-Stokes equations, assuming the smallness of $\E(r) = r^{-\frac{14}{9}} \left( \int_{Q(r)} |\nabla v|^{\frac95} dx dt \right)^\frac{10}{9}$ instead of $E(r) = \frac{1}{r} \int_{Q(r)} |\nabla v|^2 dxdt$ (see Lemmas 2.2, 2.2 and 3 for details). Note that the quantity $\E$ was already used by Choe and Lewis in [8]. The main novelty here is the iteration argument.

Next, we turn to our second main result concerning quantitative intervals of regularity. It is well-known that one *cannot* expect regularity estimates only in terms of the local kinetic and dissipation energies due to the supercritical nature of the Navier-Stokes equations. In the next result, based on the quantitative method described above, we show that such regularity estimates are nevertheless valid in certain *intervals of regularity* for any local suitable weak solution. Let $v$ be a local suitable weak solution in $Q(1)$ and $\pi_3$ be the projection map to the $x_3$-axis. According to Theorem 1, the 1D Hausdorff measure of $\pi_3(\mathcal{S}[v]) = \{-1<z<1: \R^2 \times\{z\} \times \R \cap \mathcal{S}[v] \neq \emptyset\}$ must be zero. Note that $\pi_3(\mathcal{S}[v] \cap \overline{Q(\rho)})$ is a closed set for any $\rho<1$. Hence, for any open interval $(a,b) \subset (-1,1)$, there exists a subinterval $(z_1, z_2) \subset (a,b)$ such that $v$ is regular in the strip $\{(x,t) \in Q(\rho): z_1<x_3<z_2\}$. However, Theorem 1 does not imply any explicit lower bound on the length of $(z_1, z_2)$ or any regularity estimates in such a strip. Theorem 1.1.1 provides a quantitative description of such intervals only in terms of the natural local energies, which will be important for applications in the axially symmetric case (Theorems 1.1.2 and 1.1.2).

For comparison and also for applications in the axially symmetric case, we present a similar result concerning the existence of regular epochs (intervals in the time direction), which is less surprising and much easier to prove. Theorem 1 implies that the $\frac12$D Hausdorff measure of the set $\pi_0(\mathcal{S}[v]) = \{-1<t\le 0: \(\R^3 \times \{t\}\) \cap \mathcal{S}[v] \neq \emptyset\}$ is zero, and it turns out one can obtain Proposition 1.1.1 without using the pigeonhole principle for the hollowed dissipation energies $\EE_k$.

We mention the recent interesting work of Tao [34], where a quantitative triple-exponential improvement of the $L_t^\infty L_x^3$ regularity criterion is proved. The idea is to replace the compactness arguments and unique continuation methods in [20] by suitable quantitative counterparts. See also the works [2, 23, 1] for further developments in this direction. Note that certain quantitative annuli and epochs of regularity are proved for $L^\infty_tL^3_x$ global-in-space solutions, and played important roles in [34].

### 1.1.2 Applications in the axially symmetric case

In cylindrical coordinates $(\varrho, \theta, z)$, we have the orthonormal frame

$$e_\varrho = \( \begin{matrix}
\cos \theta \\
\sin \theta \\
0
\end{matrix}\), \quad e_\theta = \( \begin{matrix}
-\sin \theta \\
\cos \theta \\
0
\end{matrix}\), \quad e_z = \( \begin{matrix}
0 \\
0 \\
1
\end{matrix}\), \tag{9}$$

under which we can write $v = v^\varrho e_\varrho + v^\theta e_\theta + v^z e_z$. We say that $(v,p)$ is axially symmetric, if the functions $v^\varrho, v^\theta, v^z, p$ are independent of $\theta \in [0,2\pi)$. An important feature of the axially symmetric Navier-Stokes equations (ASNS) is that the scalar function $\Gamma = \varrho v^\theta$ satisfies the transport-diffusion equation

$$\partial_t \Gamma - \Delta \Gamma + \frac{2}{\varrho} \partial_\varrho \Gamma + b \cdot \nabla \Gamma = 0 \tag{10}$$

where $b = v^\varrho e_\varrho + v^z e_z$. The maximum principle for (10) gives the scale-invariant a priori bound for mild solutions to the Cauchy problem:

$$\|\Gamma(t)\|_{L^\infty(\R^3)} \le \|\Gamma(0)\|_{L^\infty(\R^3)}. \tag{11}$$

Also, by the technique of Moser iteration, $\Gamma$ is locally bounded for any axially symmetric suitable weak solution [29].

In [18], the first author together with Zhang proved global regularity for mild solutions under the assumption that $\Gamma$ enjoys a rather weak modulus of continuity $|\Gamma| \le C_* |\ln \varrho|^{-2}$ near the $z$-axis. The proof indicates that the global regularity of ASNS is of a critical nature. In [36], Wei weakened the continuity assumption to $|\Gamma| \le |\ln \varrho|^{-\frac32}$. Moreover, in [18, 36], for the Cauchy problem it is shown that when $\|\Gamma\|_{L^\infty}$ is small respect to the initial data, the mild solution stays regular for all times. However, we emphasize that the latter small-swirl regularity results rely heavily on the *global-in-space* energy estimates for the unknowns $(J, \Omega) = \(\frac{\omega^\varrho}{\varrho}, \frac{\omega^\theta}{\varrho}\)$ where $\omega = \omega^\varrho e_\varrho + \omega^\theta e_\theta + \omega^z e_z$ is the vorticity, which do not allow the use of cut-off functions in the $z$-direction. See also [21] for a related study for critical initial data.

In Section 5, as an application of Theorem 1.1.1, we prove a quantitative local small-swirl regularity criterion for ASNS. Note that it is not so difficult to prove a non-quantitative version (see Proposition 5.1) based on contradiction and compactness arguments. However, the quantification of the proof is a nontrivial task. Using Theorem 1.1.1, we resolve the difficulties in localizing the energy estimates for $(J, \Omega)$ and thus obtain:

It is desirable to replace the condition (1.1.2) by an absolute smallness assumption $\|\Gamma\|_{L^\infty(Q(1))} \le c$, where $c$ is independent of $v^{\varrho}$ and $v^z$. To the best of our knowledge, this is beyond the reach of existing methods.

An interesting application of Theorem 1.1.2 is a slightly supercritical improvement of the CKN criterion for ASNS. Although we have improved partial regularity for the general Navier-Stokes equations, we can only improve the CKN criterion in the axially symmetric case. In the important works [16, 5, 4], regularity of ASNS is proved under the pointwise Type I bound

$$|v| \le \frac{C_*}{\varrho^{\alpha} \sqrt{-t}^{1-\alpha}}, \quad \alpha \in [0,1]. \tag{12}$$

In [29], the *one-point* Type I result for suitable weak solutions to ASNS

$$\limsup_{r \to 0+} \frac{1}{r} \int_{Q(r)} |\nabla v|^2 dxdt    < +\infty \implies (0,0) \notin \mathcal{S}[v]. \tag{13}$$

is established via compactness arguments and Liouville theorem. There are a few slightly supercritical generalizations of the Type I results. A slight improvement of (12), $\alpha =0$ case, is given by Pan [24]. By the more recent works [7, 31] (and Lemma 2.2), regularity of a local suitable weak solution can be proved if, for a small $\nu>0$,

$$\sup_{w\in Q(1)} \limsup_{r \to 0+} \frac{\int_{Q(r,w)} |\nabla v|^2 dxdt}{r (\ln |\ln r|)^\nu}     < +\infty. \tag{14}$$

Our next result is a corollary of Theorem 1.1.2, from which all the (slightly supercritical) Type I results in the literature can be deduced (see Remark 5.3 for details).

Theorem 1.1.2 directly improves Seregin’s one-point result (13). Our condition (1.1.2) is much weaker than (14) since the bound is assumed only *at a single point*. We emphasize that a direct consequence of Theorem 1.1.2 or (14) reads: there exist $\kappa, \sigma>0$ such that for all $0 \le \alpha \le 1$, we have

$$|v| \le C_* \frac{ ( \ln |\ln \varrho|)^\kappa \cdot (\ln |\ln (-t)|)^\sigma }{\varrho^\alpha \sqrt{-t}^{1-\alpha}}  \ \mbox{in} \ Q(r) \ \mbox{for some} \ r>0  \implies (0,0) \notin \mathcal{S}[v].$$

This obviously improves the Type I criteria in [16, 5, 4] and generalizes the result of [24].

Finally, we point out that via standard covering arguments, Theorem 1.1.2 implies the partial regularity result $\mathcal{P}^f(\S[v]) = 0$ for $f = r(\ln |\ln r|)^\mu$, a statement weaker than Theorem 1.1.1. It is an interesting question whether (1.1.2) still holds true with $(\ln |\ln r|)^\mu$ in the denominator replaced by $|\ln r|$. We also mention that the recent numerical results [13] seem to suggest that ASNS may develop singularity in a nearly self-similar scenario where the blow-up rate is Type I with some logarithmic corrections.

## 1.2 Organization

In Section 2, we introduce the notations to be used throughout the paper, and state a few preliminary lemmas on scale-invariant quantities and coverings. In Section 3, we use a quantitative version of the CKN criterion and the pigeonhole principle to prove Theorem 1.1.1. In Section 4, we prove the quantitative results concerning the intervals and epochs of regularity, *i.e.*, Theorem 1.1.1 and Proposition 1.1.1. In Section 5, for comparison, we first prove a non-quantitative version of Theorem 1.1.2 using a compactness argument. Then we apply the results of Section 4 to show Theorem 1.1.2. Theorem 1.1.2 is finally deduced as a corollary of Theorem 1.1.2. The proofs of the auxilliary Lemmas 5.2 & 5.2 are given in the Appendix.

# 2 Preliminaries

## 2.1 Notations

- We write $c, C$ or $O(1)$ for positive absolute constants whose values may vary from line to line. We write $X \lesssim Y$ for $X \le CY$. $X \sim Y$ stands for $X \lesssim Y$ and $Y \lesssim X$. $O_m(1)$ stands for a positive constant which depends only on $m$. $X \lesssim_m Y$ means that $X \le O_m(1) \, Y$.

- For a point $w = (x,t) \in \R^3 \times \R$, we denote

$$B(r, x) = \{y \in \R^3: |x-y|<r\},$$

and

$$Q(r,w) = B(r,x) \times (-r^2 + t, t).$$

For simplicity, we write $Q(r) = Q(r,(0,0))$ and $B(r) = B(r, (0,0))$. We also need $Q^+(r,w) = B(r,x) \times (-r^2+t, r^2+t)$.

- We shall use the following scale-invariant quantities.

$$\begin{equation*}
  A(r) = \mathop{\mathrm{ess\,sup}}_{t \in (-r^2, 0)} \frac{1}{r} \int_{B(r)} |v(x,t)|^2 dx, \quad E(r) = \frac{1}{r} \int_{Q(r)} |\nabla v|^2 dxdt,
  \end{equation*}$$

$$\begin{equation*}
  F(r) = \frac{1}{r^2} \int_{Q(r)} |v(x,t)|^3 dxdt, \quad D(r) = \frac{1}{r^2} \int_{Q(r)} |p(x,t)|^\frac32 dxdt,
  \end{equation*}$$

$$\E(r) = r^{-\frac{14}{9}} \left( \int_{Q(r)} |\nabla v|^{\frac95} dx dt \right)^{\frac{10}{9}}. \tag{15}$$

Using Hölder’s inequality, it is clear that

$$\E(r) \le \(\frac43 \pi\)^{\frac19} E(r). \tag{16}$$

$A(r,w), E(r,w)$, *etc.* will denote the corresponding scale-invariant quantities for $Q(r,w)$ instead of $Q(r)$. Moreover, we introduce

$$E^+(r,w) =  \frac{1}{r} \int_{Q^+(r,w) \cap Q(1)} |\nabla v|^2 dxdt.$$

- We use the usual notations $L^s_t L^l_x$ for the spacetime mixed Lebesgue spaces, *e.g.*,

$$\|v\|_{L^\infty_t L^2_x(Q(1))} = \mathop{\mathrm{ess\,sup}}_{-1<t<0} \(\int |v|^2 dx \)^\frac12. \tag{17}$$

For simplicity, we write $L^s(Q(1)) = L_t^s L_x^s(Q(1))$.

## 2.2 Iteration of scale-invariant quantities

We start with the iterations of scale-invariant quantities similar to those in [20, 17]. We shall see that in many of such estimates, the scale-invariant quantity $E$ which plays an important role can be replaced by $\E$.

*Proof.* We only prove the estimates involving $\E$, since the estimates involving $E$ are more standard and follow from the same method. Let $[v]_\rho$ be the mean value of $v$ on $B(\rho)$, then by Hölder’s inequality, for $-\rho^2<t<0$,

$$\begin{align*}
[v]_\rho(t)   \lesssim  \frac{1}{\rho^{\frac32}} \(\int_{B(\rho)} |v|^2 dx\)^{\frac12} \le \frac{1}{\rho} A^{\frac12}(\rho), \tag{18}\end{align*}$$

and

$$\begin{align*}
[v]_\rho(t)   \lesssim  \frac{1}{\rho} \(\int_{B(\rho)} |v|^3 dx\)^{\frac13} \tag{19}\end{align*}$$

Hence, we have

$$\begin{align*}
\frac{1}{r^2} \int_{Q(r)} |[v]_\rho|^3 dxdt \lesssim  \( \frac{r}{\rho} \)^3 \min \{ F(\rho), A^{\frac32}(\rho) \}. \tag{20}\end{align*}$$

We estimate $F(r)$ using interpolation and the Sobolev embedding $W^{1,{\frac95}}_x \hookrightarrow L^{\frac92}_x$,

$$\begin{align*}
 
F(r) &= \frac{1}{r^2} \int_{Q(r)} |v|^3 dxdt  \\
&\lesssim \frac{1}{r^2} \int_{Q(r)} |[v]_\rho|^3 dxdt  + \frac{1}{r^2} \int_{Q(r)} |v - [v]_\rho|^3 dxdt \\
&\lesssim  \( \frac{r}{\rho} \)^3 \min \{ F(\rho), A^{\frac32}(\rho) \}  +  \frac{1}{r^2} \|v-[v]_\rho\|_{L^\infty_t L^2_x(Q(\rho))}^{\frac65} \|v-[v]_\rho\|_{L^{\frac95}_t L^{\frac92}_x(Q(\rho))}^{\frac95}  \\
&\lesssim  \( \frac{r}{\rho} \)^3 \min \{ F(\rho), A^{\frac32}(\rho) \}  +  \frac{1}{r^2} \|v-[v]_\rho\|_{L^\infty_t L^2_x(Q(\rho))}^{\frac65} \|\nabla v\|_{L^{\frac95}_t L^{\frac95}_x(Q(\rho))}^{\frac95}  \\
&\lesssim \( \frac{r}{\rho} \)^3 \min \{ F(\rho), A^{\frac32}(\rho) \} + \( \frac{\rho}{r} \)^2  A^{\frac35}(\rho) \E^{\frac{9}{10}}(\rho). \tag{21}\end{align*}$$

To estimate $D(r)$, we use the well-known decomposition of pressure

$$p = p_1 + p_2, \tag{22}$$

with $p_1$ is given by

$$p_1 = -\Delta^{-1} \mbox{div} \mbox{div} \( \mathbf{1}_{B(\rho)} (v-[v]_{\rho})\otimes(v-[v]_{\rho})\) \tag{23}$$

for each time $-\rho^2<t<0$. Clearly, $p_2$ is harmonic in space, hence

$$\begin{align*}
\int_{Q(r)} |p_2|^{\frac32} \le \left(\frac{r}{\rho}\right)^3 \int_{Q(\rho)} |p_2|^{\frac32}. \tag{24}\end{align*}$$

By the theory of singular integrals, $p_1$ satisfies the estimate

$$\begin{align*}
 
\int_{Q(\rho)} |p_1|^{\frac32} \lesssim \int_{Q(\rho)} |v-[v]_{B_\sigma(\rho)}|^3. \tag{25}\end{align*}$$

As we have shown in (2.2),

$$\begin{align*}
 
\int_{Q(\rho)} |v-[v]_{B_\sigma(\rho)}|^3 \lesssim \rho^2 A^{\frac35}(\rho) \E^{\frac{9}{10}}(\rho). \tag{26}\end{align*}$$

Hence, combining the above estimates, we have

$$\begin{align*}
D(r) &= \frac{1}{r^2} \int_{Q(r)} |p|^{\frac32} dxdt  \\
&\lesssim \frac{1}{r^2} \int_{Q(r)} |p_1|^{\frac32} dxdt + \frac{1}{r^2} \int_{Q(r)} |p_2|^{\frac32} dxdt  \\
&\lesssim  \(\frac{1}{r^2} + \frac{r}{\rho^3}\) \int_{Q(r)} |p_1|^{\frac32} dxdt + \frac{r}{\rho^3} \int_{Q(\rho)} |p|^{\frac32} dxdt  \\
&\lesssim \(\frac{\rho}{r}\)^2 A^{\frac35}(\rho) \E^{\frac{9}{10}}(\rho) + \frac{r}{\rho} D(\rho). \tag{27}\end{align*}$$

*Proof.* We only prove the estimate involving $\E$, since the others are standard. By taking an appropriate test function in the local energy inequality (1), and using interpolation, we have

$$\begin{align*}
A(r) + E(r) &\lesssim \frac{1}{r^3} \int_{Q(2r)} |v|^2 dxdt + \frac{1}{r^2} \int_{Q(2r)} |v|\(|v|^2 - [|v|^2]_{2r} + 2p\) \\
& \lesssim  F^{\frac23}(2r) + \frac{1}{r^2} \(\int_{Q(2r)}|v|^3 dxdt\)^{\frac13}  \(\int_{Q(2r)} \(|v|^2 - [|v|^2]_{2r} \)^{\frac32} dxdt\)^{\frac23} + \\
&\quad + \frac{1}{r^2} \(\int_{Q(2r)}|v|^3 dxdt\)^{\frac13}  \(\int_{Q(2r)} |p|^{\frac32} dxdt\)^{\frac23} \\
&\lesssim  F^{\frac23}(2r) + \frac{F^{\frac13}(2r)}{r^{\frac43}}  \(\int_{-4r^2}^0 \(\int_{B(2r)} |v| |\nabla v| dx\)^{\frac32} dt\)^{\frac23} + \\
&\quad + F^{\frac13}(2r) D^{\frac23}(2r) \\
&\lesssim  F^{\frac23}(2r) + \frac{F^{\frac13}(2r)}{r^{\frac43}}  \|v\|^{\frac23}_{L_t^\infty L_x^2(Q(2r))} \|v\|^{\frac13}_{L_t^3 L_x^3(Q(2r))} \|\nabla v\|_{L_t^{\frac95}L_x^{\frac95}(Q(2r))} + \\
&\quad + F^{\frac13}(2r) D^{\frac23}(2r) \\
&\lesssim  F^{\frac23}(2r) + F^{\frac49}(2r)  A^{\frac13}(2r) \E^{\frac12}(2r) + F^{\frac13}(2r) D^{\frac23}(2r). 
\end{align*}$$

*Proof.* Without loss of generality, we let $w = (0, 0)$. Consider the logarithmic case (2.2) first. Using Lemma 2.2, for a small number $\theta>0$ there holds

$$\begin{align*}
 
F(\theta r) &\le \frac{1}{16} F\(\frac{r}{2}\) + C_\theta A^\frac12\(\frac{r}{2}\) E\(\frac{r}{2}\) \le  \frac14 F(r) + C |\ln r| A^\frac12\(\frac{r}{2}\), \tag{28}\end{align*}$$

and

$$\begin{align*}
 
D(\theta r) &\le \frac1{16} D\(\frac{r}{2}\) + C_\theta A^\frac12\(\frac{r}{2}\) E\(\frac{r}{2}\) \le \frac14 D(r) + C |\ln r| A^\frac12\(\frac{r}{2}\). \tag{29}\end{align*}$$

Using Lemma 2.2, we have

$$A\(\frac{r}{2}\)  \le C (F(r)+D(r)+1). \tag{30}$$

Combining (28)–(30), we arrive at

$$F(\theta r ) + D(\theta r) \le \frac12 (F(r) + D(r)) + C |\ln r|^2. \tag{31}$$

An induction using (31) gives, for sufficiently small $r$,

$$F(r ) + D( r) \le C |\ln r|^2,$$

which, together with (30), implies (2.2).

The proof for the double logarithmic case (2.2) $\implies$ (2.2) is similar. ◻

# 3 Improved partial regularity

## 5.1 A non-quantitative result

Before embarking on the proof of the quantitative Theorem 1.1.2, we present a non-quantitative version of it whose proof relies on a compactness argument. However, we emphasize that a direct quantification of this proof is a nontrivial task.

*Proof.* We argue by contradiction and follow the stability of singularity argument in [26, Lemma 2.1]. Suppose that the conclusion is wrong, then there exist a sequence of axially symmetric local suitable weak solutions $v_k, p_k$ in $Q(1)$ with

$$\iint_{Q_1} |v_k|^3 + |p_k|^\frac32 \le \G < + \infty,$$

and

$$|\Gamma_k|_{L^\infty} \le \e_k \to 0,$$

and a sequence of points $w_k \in \overline{Q(\frac12)}$ such that $w_k$ is a singular point of $v_k$. Up to taking subsequences we have the convergences (see [17, Page 367] for the discussion on compactness)

$$w_k \to w_\infty \in \overline{Q\Big(\frac12\Big)},$$

and

$$v_k \to v_\infty \mathrm{\ strongly \ in\ } L_t^{3}L_x^{3}\Big(Q\Big(\frac23\Big)\Big).$$

Note that $v_\infty$ is a suitable weak solution with no swirl ($v_\infty^\theta = 0$). It is known that $v_\infty$ must be regular (see, *e.g.*, [15]), and thus

$$\|v_\infty\|_{L^\infty(Q(\frac23))} \le A$$

for some finite number $A$. Let $a(A)> b(A)> 0$ be small numbers to be chosen later. Using the convergence of $v_k \to v_\infty$, we have, for large $k$,

$$\int_{ B_a(0) \times (-b^2, 0)  + w_\infty} |v_k|^3 dxdt \le 2A a^3 b^2$$

and

$$\int_{Q(b,w_\infty)} |v_k|^3  dxdt < 2A b^5$$

Then, using the usual decomposition of $p_k$ (see the proof of Lemma 2.2) in the domain $B_a(0) \times (-b^2, 0)  + w_\infty$, we have

$$p_k = p_{k1} + p_{k2} \tag{80}$$

where $\Delta p_{k1} = 0$ and

$$\int_{B_a(0) \times (-b^2, 0)  + w_\infty} |p_{k2}|^\frac32 dxdt \lesssim \int_{B_a(0) \times (-b^2, 0)  + w_\infty} |v_k|^3  dxdt \tag{81}$$

Consequently, we obtain

$$\begin{align*}
\int_{Q(b,w_\infty)}|p_k|^\frac32 dxdt &\lesssim \int_{Q(b,w_\infty)}|p_{k1}|^\frac32 dxdt + \int_{Q(b,w_\infty)}|p_{k2}|^\frac32 dxdt \\
&\lesssim \frac{b^3}{a^3} \int_{B_a(0) \times (-b^2, 0)  + w_\infty} |p_{k1}|^\frac32 dxdt + \int_{B_a(0) \times (-b^2, 0)  + w_\infty} |p_{k2}|^\frac32 dxdt \\
&\lesssim \frac{b^3}{a^3} \int_{Q(1)} |p_{k}|^\frac32 dxdt + \int_{B_a(0) \times (-b^2, 0)  + w_\infty} |p_{k2}|^\frac32 dxdt \\
&\lesssim \frac{\G b^3}{a^3} + A a^3 b^2.
\end{align*}$$

By taking $a(A), b(A)$ suitably small, we get

$$\int_{Q(b,w_\infty)} |v_k|^3 + |p_k|^\frac32 \, dxdt \le \varepsilon_* b^2$$

where $\varepsilon_*$ is from Theorem 1. This contradicts with the assumption that $w_k$ is a singular point of $v_k$. Hence, the proposition is proved. ◻
